en: The carabao, the Philippine national animal, wallows in mud to cool its body because it lacks sufficient sweat glands.
The narra, the Philippine national tree, produces small winged seeds that spin like helicopter blades as they fall to the soil.
The sampaguita, the national flower, releases its strongest sweet fragrance at night to attract moth pollinators in the local environment.
The Ifugao people maintain the muyong system, a traditional forest management practice above their rice terraces that naturally filters and stores rainwater.
The historic banyan tree in Kawit, Cavite, features aerial roots that absorb moisture directly from the humid tropical air.
During the Pahiyas Festival, farmers decorate their homes with kiping, which are vibrant, leaf-shaped wafers made from pounded rice grains.
National Scientist Julian Banzon researched how to extract fuel and industrial chemicals from the cellulose of locally grown abaca and coconut plants.
The Department of Environment and Natural Resources protects the Philippine crocodile, which can be observed basking in the freshwater marshes of Maramag.
The Philippine eagle, the national bird, requires large dipterocarp forest canopies to hunt for flying lemurs and other arboreal prey.
The T'boli indigenous group creates traditional t'nalak cloth by extracting strong fibers from abaca stalks and dyeing them with native roots and leaves.
National Scientist Alfredo Santos isolated medicinal alkaloid compounds from the leaves of the sambong, a common shrub in Philippine backyards.
The traditional bayanihan practice of moving houses relied on the strong, flexible structural properties of locally harvested bamboo poles.
